claims.text: The proposed method uses a machine-learning potential trained with density-functional-theory calculations and molecular-dynamics simulations.
Neural-network potentials and Gaussian-process regression are proposed as candidate machine-learning approaches.
The proposed potential will incorporate vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The machine-learning potential will capture the structural and thermodynamic properties of solid and fluid high-entropy systems near phase transitions.
Learning relationships between structural and thermodynamic properties will reduce the need for costly explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will accurately predict thermodynamic properties near phase transitions.
The method will reduce computational cost by 50–70% relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The method will improve throughput by 20–30% relative to TOR-TILD for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The method will achieve 90–95% fidelity relative to explicit ab initio results.
Fidelity will be assessed using mean absolute error in predicted thermodynamic properties.
The proposed temperature domain is 500–2000 K near phase transitions.
The method is expected to apply to systems containing up to five components.
TiZrHfNbTa and AlCoCrFeNi are proposed as systems within the method's applicability domain.
Performance depends on the quality of the training data and the potential's ability to represent complex structure–thermodynamics relationships.
The method may fail at very high temperatures or for very complex phase transitions.

The hypothesis is to be falsified if the method fails to achieve a 30% cost reduction or a 10% throughput improvement relative to TOR-TILD, or if fidelity relative to explicit ab initio results is below 85%.

contradictions.description: The initial state labels elemental and binary systems as high-entropy systems, whereas the boundary and examples frame the target as multicomponent high-entropy systems; the intended material class is therefore internally unclear.

The predicted 50–70% cost reduction is explicitly relative to ab initio molecular dynamics, but the falsification rule applies a 30% cost-reduction threshold relative to TOR-TILD. This changes the cost comparator and does not directly test the stated cost prediction.
